pages.description: The Hebrew screen-reader journey run by Guidepup under VoiceOver and NVDA, and the accessibility-tree snapshots that run with every end-to-end test.
pages.md:
Automated checks such as axe find only part of what blocks a screen reader
user. Lumen checks screen-reader output at two levels.

## 1. Accessibility-tree snapshots (every e2e run)

`e2e/aria-hebrew.spec.ts` pins what a screen reader receives in the Hebrew
interface: roles, names and states. It uses Playwright's aria snapshots on
Chromium, with no screen reader needed:

- the skip link comes before the main landmark;
- a note's headings carry their levels, task checkboxes their state, and links their names;
- the command palette is a named modal dialog with a search box and results as options;
- the keyboard-shortcuts dialog is named and has a heading.

```sh
npx playwright test e2e/aria-hebrew.spec.ts --project=chromium
```

## 2. Real screen readers (Guidepup, on a Mac or Windows)

`sr/` runs ten tasks of the screen reader protocol (plan W1.23)
with [Guidepup](https://www.guidepup.dev/) (MIT). Guidepup drives VoiceOver
or NVDA and records what it says. Each task passes when the Hebrew it must
hear was spoken. The tasks are in `sr/journey.ts`.

Guidepup needs a real desktop: it takes over the screen reader, the keyboard
and the audio. It does not run in CI containers or in the cloud sandbox.

### On a Mac (VoiceOver)

```sh
npm install -D @guidepup/guidepup @guidepup/playwright @guidepup/setup   # once
npx @guidepup/setup                                       # once: lets VoiceOver be scripted
npm run test:sr -- --project=voiceover
```

Set the VoiceOver voice to Carmit (Hebrew) in VoiceOver Utility first.

### On Windows or a Windows VM (NVDA)

```sh
npm install -D @guidepup/guidepup @guidepup/playwright   # once
npx @guidepup/setup                                       # once: installs a portable NVDA
npm run test:sr -- --project=nvda-chrome
npm run test:sr -- --project=nvda-firefox
```

Set NVDA's voice to a Hebrew one (eSpeak NG Hebrew or Microsoft Asaf).

### Every night on the Mac

Once the three `@guidepup/*` packages are installed, `npm run nightly` on
the Mac (plan W4.36, [the nightly runs](/contributing/nightly/)) adds the
**sr** kind: `npx @guidepup/setup --ci`, then the VoiceOver journey. The
sealed report `reports/nightly/<date>-sr.json` holds, per setup, the tasks
passed, each blocker and the protocol row. `npm run nightly -- --only sr`
runs it alone.

The nightly needs the Mac logged in (VoiceOver speaks only in a user
session) with the screen unlocked. If System Integrity Protection is on,
`@guidepup/setup` can't write the permission itself: once, in System
Settings → Privacy & Security, give the terminal that runs the nightly
**Accessibility** and **Automation → VoiceOver**, and in VoiceOver Utility
turn on **Allow VoiceOver to be controlled with AppleScript**.

### Results

Each run prints a row for the protocol's results table, for example
`| 2026-11-12 | 0.1.0 | NVDA / Windows / chromium (Guidepup) | 10/10 (…) | — |`.
It also writes `sr-results/results.json`, with every phrase spoken in each
task. Paste the row into the protocol's results table and update the
accessibility conformance report from it. TalkBack stays a manual check,
once per release.

pages.title: Screen reader protocol
pages.description: The fixed Hebrew journey run with NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack before a release, and its results.
pages.md:
Automated checks such as axe find only part of what blocks a screen reader
user. This journey is run by a person, **without looking at the screen**,
with each screen reader, in **Hebrew** (Hebrew interface, Hebrew voice).
A step passes when it is done with the screen reader alone. A **blocker** is
a step that cannot be done at all. The release target is **0 blockers**
on every screen reader.

## Setups

| Screen reader | System | Browser | Voice |
|---|---|---|---|
| NVDA 2025.x | Windows 11 | Firefox and Chrome | eSpeak NG or Microsoft Asaf (Hebrew) |
| VoiceOver | macOS 15+ | Safari | Carmit (Hebrew) |
| VoiceOver | iOS 18+ | Safari | Carmit (Hebrew) |
| TalkBack | Android 14+ | Chrome | Google TTS, Hebrew |

Before starting: in Lumen, set the language to עברית (Settings → Language,
or the setup) and clear the site data so the first run starts fresh.

## The journey

1. **Start.** Open the app. The page title and the editor's name are read.
2. **Skip link.** Tab once: "Skip to the editor" is read; Enter moves focus into the editor.
3. **Write.** Type `# תוכנית`, Enter, then a line of Hebrew text. The text is read as typed, in Hebrew.
4. **Structure.** Arrow up to the first line: "כותרת 1: תוכנית" is read.
5. **Task.** Add `- [ ] לקנות חלב`, arrow away and back: "משימה, לא בוצעה" is read.
6. **Where am I.** Open the palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K), type `מיקום`, Enter: the line, the column and the heading are read.
7. **Palette.** In the palette, arrow through the results: each command's name is read, and the number of results is read when it changes.
8. **Dialog.** Open the keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+/ / ⌘/). The dialog's name is read, Tab stays inside, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the editor.
9. **Search.** Open search, type a word from the note, open the result: the note opens and focus is in the editor.
10. **Sidebar.** Open the workspace sidebar from the palette, move through the files and open one.
11. **Preview.** Switch to preview (from the palette). Headings can be listed with the screen reader's headings list, in order.
12. **AI.** If AI is set up: run a writing command. "ה-AI עובד…" and then "ה-AI סיים." are read, and the result can be reached.
13. **Mixed direction.** A line with Hebrew and an English word is read in the right order.
14. **Settings.** Open theme settings, switch to dark mode and back with the keyboard. Each control's state is read.

## Results

Each run adds a row: the date, the Lumen version, the setup, the steps that
passed, and each blocker with a link to its issue.

| Date | Version | Setup | Passed | Blockers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | 0.1.0 | NVDA / Windows | not run yet | — |
| — | 0.1.0 | VoiceOver / macOS | not run yet | — |
| — | 0.1.0 | VoiceOver / iOS | not run yet | — |
| — | 0.1.0 | TalkBack / Android | not run yet | — |

pages.title: Testing with screen reader users
pages.description: The kit for sessions with three Hebrew screen reader users — who to ask, the invitation, consent, the tasks, how a session is scored, and what happens to each barrier.
pages.md:
axe and the scripted readers find only part of what blocks people. Israeli
Standard 5568 is about real use, so before a release the
[screen reader protocol](/editor/screen-reader-protocol/) is also done by
**three people who use a screen reader every day, in Hebrew**. This page is
the kit for those sessions. The project owner recruits and runs them.

## Who

Three participants, one per setup, so every common reader is covered:

| Participant | Screen reader | System |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | NVDA (or JAWS) | Windows, Chrome or Firefox |
| 2 | VoiceOver | macOS or iPhone, Safari |
| 3 | TalkBack | Android, Chrome |

Each one uses the screen reader daily for at least a year and reads Hebrew
with it. No experience with Lumen or with Markdown is needed: the session
explains the four Markdown marks it uses.

## Organisations to ask

These Israeli organisations work with blind and low-vision people and with
digital accessibility. Ask them to pass the invitation on. Don't ask them
for anyone's contact details.

- **Migdal Or** (מגדלור), rehabilitation centre for the blind. It runs a
  national technology helpline staffed by blind and low-vision specialists,
  and accessibility checks for employers.
- **The Center for the Blind in Israel** (המרכז לעיוור בישראל).
- **Access Israel** (נגישות ישראל), aisrael.org. It runs usability testing
  with people with disabilities.
- **The Central Library for the Blind, Visually Impaired and Handicapped**,
  clfb.org.il. Its readers are experienced screen reader users.

## Compensation

A token payment, a gift card of 150–250 ₪ for a session of about an hour,
or a donation in the participant's name to one of the organisations above.
Volunteering is also fine if the participant prefers it. Say which in the
invitation.

## The invitation

> Lumen is a free, open-source note editor that works in Hebrew and runs on
> your own device. We're looking for three people who use NVDA, JAWS,
> VoiceOver or TalkBack every day, in Hebrew, for a one-hour session (online
> or in person). You'll do ten everyday tasks, like writing a note,
> finding one and changing a setting, while thinking aloud. We're testing
> the app, not you. Every barrier you hit will be fixed before the next
> release. [Payment: gift card of ___ ₪ / donation / volunteer.] Reply to
> ___ to take part.

## Consent

Before the session, read this to the participant and note their answer:

- Taking part is voluntary. They can stop at any time without giving a
  reason, and still receive the payment.
- With their permission, the screen and the screen reader's speech are
  recorded. The recording is used only to fix barriers and is deleted
  within 90 days. Without permission, only written notes are kept.
- Their name is not published. The results table shows the setup only.

## The session

Use the 14 steps of the [screen reader protocol](/editor/screen-reader-protocol/).
Pick the 10 everyday ones: steps 1–9 and 14. Give each task in words, not
key names. Example: "Write a note called תוכנית with a heading and one task".
Then wait.

For each task, write down:

- **done** (alone), **done with a hint**, or **not done** (a **blocker**)
- what the participant expected and what the reader said instead

A session passes when the participant completes **8 or more of the 10**
tasks unaided. The goal for the release is **3 sessions passed, and every
blocker fixed**.

## After the session

1. Open one [accessibility report](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/issues/new?template=accessibility.yml)
   per blocker, with the setup, the task and what the reader said.
2. Add a row to the protocol's results table: date, version, setup
   (people), tasks passed, the blockers with their issue links.
3. When a blocker's fix ships, ask the participant, if they agree, to
   check that task again.

## Accessibility statement

The [accessibility statement](/editor/accessibility-statement/) is the
document regulation 35 of the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities
(service accessibility adjustments) regulations, 2013 asks for. It must
name the standard (IS 5568, which adopts WCAG 2.0 AA), say what is
accessible and what is not yet, give a way to report a barrier and the
accessibility coordinator, and show when it was last reviewed. Update the
statement after each round of sessions. Part 2 of IS 5568 (September 2023)
covers documents people download, such as Word and PDF files. It applies
to the files Lumen exports. Check an export against it when its format
changes.

pages.title: Settings
pages.description: One screen for every setting — tabs, search, and export / import of your choices.
pages.md:
Open **Settings** from the command palette (`⌘K` → *Settings*). Every
older settings dialog now opens here, on its own tab:

| Tab | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| General | View mode, theme, language, text direction, panels, editor switches (Vim, typewriter, spelling, grammar, TypeScript checks, suggesting), auto-save, daily writing goal, local AI, error reports |
| Theme | Accent color, fonts, size, line height, content width, presets |
| AI settings | AI policy and cost mode, who runs the agents, Ollama address and model, the model manager (downloads, storage), local grammar and research services, writing style |
| Collaboration settings | Signaling server, public signaling fallback, persistent server and its token |
| Train AI on my style | Fine-tuned model and whether AI requests use it |
| Trusted signing keys | The Ed25519 keys plugins must be signed with |
| Organization | Name, allowed email domains, SSO, audit log |

## Search

Type in the search box at the top. Lumen matches the name of every
setting — including the ones inside a tab, such as *Ollama* or
*signaling* — and shows only the tabs that have a match. In the General
tab, only the matching settings stay on screen.

## Export and import

**Export JSON** downloads `lumen-settings.json` with your choices. It never
contains:

- API keys, tokens or passwords;
- your notes, open tabs, caches or history;
- the trusted plugin-signing keys or the organization policy.

**Import JSON** reads such a file back. Each value is checked against the
settings table: an unknown name, a secret, or a value of the wrong type is
skipped, and the toast tells you how many settings were imported and how
many were skipped. An import never loosens the AI policy: a file that says
*Cloud* doesn't move a device that keeps AI on this device to the cloud —
change that yourself in the AI tab.

## For developers

Every stored key and every persisted store field is listed in
`src/settings/schema.ts`, with its kind (`setting`, `secret` or `data`),
its tab and its label. `src/__tests__/settingsSchema.test.ts` scans the
sources and fails when a new key is missing from the table, so the screen,
its search and its export can't fall behind.

pages.title: Smart Insert (⌘⇧V)
pages.description: Paste anything into one dialog — Lumen detects the type and wraps it in the right block.
pages.md:
`⌘⇧V` opens a single dialog with one big text area. Paste **anything**
and Lumen figures out what to do with it — across 19 detectors, from
specific (a YouTube URL) to general (a code block whose language is
sniffed from the content).

## The detectors, in order

| Order | Match | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | YouTube / Vimeo / Spotify / Twitter / TikTok / Reddit / GitHub Gist / Figma / Maps / 8 more | ` ```embed ` |
| 2 | Bare HTTPS URL on a single line | Markdown link `[url](url)` |
| 3 | `$$…$$` or `\begin{equation}…\end{equation}` | Math fence |
| 4 | `flowchart LR …`, `sequenceDiagram`, `gantt`, … | ` ```mermaid ` |
| 5 | `digraph G { … }` | ` ```dot ` |
| 6 | `@startuml … @enduml` | ` ```plantuml ` |
| 7 | `X:1 T:Test K:C …` (ABC notation) | ` ```abc ` |
| 8 | `@article{…}` | ` ```bibtex ` |
| 9 | `{ "type": "FeatureCollection", … }` | ` ```map ` (GeoJSON) |
| 10 | YAML with `view:` + `type:` / `source:` | ` ```database ` |
| 11 | YAML with `series:` + `xAxis:` | ` ```chart ` |
| 12 | `CREATE TABLE / INSERT INTO / SELECT …` | ` ```sql ` (parsed to table) |
| 13 | JSON array of homogeneous objects | ` ```json-table ` |
| 14 | Other valid JSON | ` ```json ` |
| 15 | HTML with `<script>` / `<svg>` / `<canvas>` | ` ```htmlpreview ` (interactive iframe) |
| 16 | Other static HTML | Converted to markdown |
| 17 | `name,age\nalice,30\n…` | ` ```csv ` (table + chart suggestions) |
| 18 | Tab-separated rows | ` ```tsv ` |
| 19 | Code that sniffs as JS / TS / Python / Rust / Go / Java / C / C++ / PHP / Ruby / Dockerfile | ` ```<lang> ` |
| 20 | Anything else | Plain markdown — inserted as-is |

The first match wins. The detection badge in the dialog shows you
exactly what was identified ("Detected as: 🔗 YouTube embed") and a
dropdown lets you override.

## The preview pane

The dialog renders the converted markdown in a preview area below the
input. Live-updates as you type. You see exactly what's about to land
in the doc before you commit with ⌘↵.

## Insert position

- **At cursor** — uses the editor's exposed `insertText` handle so the
  surrounding selection is replaced cleanly.
- **Append** — adds to the end of the doc with two newlines.
- **Replace** — swaps the entire doc (use sparingly).

## Examples

> Paste "https://twitter.com/elonmusk/status/1585841080431321088"

→ Detected as: 🐦 X / Twitter embed → wraps as ```` ```embed ````.

> Paste "name,age\\nalice,30\\nbob,25"

→ Detected as: 📊 CSV table → wraps as ```` ```csv ```` and Lumen
suggests a bar chart based on the column types.

> Paste a multi-line `function fetch(url) { … }`

→ Detected as: 💻 JS code → wraps as ```` ```js ```` with Shiki
highlighting.

## Keyboard shortcut

`⌘⇧V` everywhere. Also reachable via:

- The toolbar's **Insert** menu → first item, marked with ✨.
- The command palette (`⌘K`), search "insert anything".

pages.md:
**Settings → Theme** (command palette: *Theme settings*) changes how Lumen
looks, live, without a reload: a theme switch takes one frame.

## Built-in themes

| Theme | For |
|---|---|
| Default | Lumen's own light and dark palette |
| Sepia | warm paper, low glare |
| Nord | cool blue-grey |
| High contrast | black on white and white on black, text at 7:1 |
| **Ktav (Hebrew reading)** | paper and ink, a Hebrew serif in the editor and the preview, more space between lines |

Every theme passes WCAG AA in both light and dark mode: body and muted text
at 4.5:1 or more against the background, the accent at 3:1, and text on the
accent at 4.5:1. The **Contrast** section of the settings shows the numbers
for what you have chosen, including your own accent colour.

**Ktav** sets the editor and the preview to a Hebrew serif that ships with
the system (Frank Ruehl CLM, David, Noto Serif Hebrew, then Times New
Roman), 16 px, with a line height of 1.85 and a 70-character measure. You
can change any of these after choosing the theme.

## Theme files and the tokens

**Export** saves your theme as JSON; **Import** reads one back, strictly
validated (8 KB at most, unknown keys refused). A theme only sets the
documented tokens: the custom properties below, consumed as
`hsl(var(--token))`.

| Token | Is |
|---|---|
| `--bg`, `--bg-subtle`, `--bg-muted`, `--bg-inset` | backgrounds, from the page to inset wells |
| `--fg`, `--fg-subtle`, `--fg-muted` | text, from body text to hints |
| `--border`, `--border-strong` | lines |
| `--accent`, `--accent-fg` | links, focus, buttons; text on the accent |
| `--editor-font`, `--editor-font-size`, `--editor-line-height` | the editor's type |
| `--content-width`, `--preview-width` | the measure of the editor and the preview |
| `--font-serif`, `--preview-line-height` | the preview's type (set by Ktav) |

The design system's other tokens — spacing, radii, shadows, motion — are
listed in *Contributing → Design system*; snippets can use them too.

## CSS snippets

Put `.css` files in the vault's `.lumen/snippets/` folder (Lumen also reads
`.obsidian/snippets/`, so a vault from Obsidian keeps its snippets). Each one
appears under **CSS snippets** in the theme settings with a switch. Changes
to the files apply as you save them.

Snippets can restyle anything, but **they can't load anything from the
network**. Before a snippet reaches the page, Lumen reads it the way the
browser does and removes:

- every `@import`;
- any declaration with `url()`, `image-set()`, `image()`, `cross-fade()`,
  `element()` or `attr(… url)` pointing anywhere but a `data:` image or font
  or a `#fragment`. That holds however it is written: `URL(`, `u\72l(`, quoted or
  not, inside a custom property or a `var()` fallback;
- old script hooks (`expression()`, `behavior`, `-moz-binding`) and
  `@document`.

The settings list what was removed, with the line and the reason. The
page's Content Security Policy is a second line, but on its own it would
allow a stylesheet to load images from any HTTPS site, so the sanitizer is
what keeps snippets off the network. As a third line, Lumen watches for any
request a stylesheet makes to another site, and the **privacy ledger**
would show it. Its tests check that a snippet full of remote URLs makes no
request at all.

pages.md:
Each of these has a **?** button that opens this help at its own section.

## Theme settings

**Theme settings…** in the command palette changes the colours, the
accent, the editor's font, size and line height, and the width of the
text, live. The **Contrast** section shows whether the text and the
accent are readable against the background. **Export** saves the theme as a
file and **Import** reads one back.

## Voice memos and dictation

Speak instead of typing. The quick mode writes what you say straight into
the note with the browser's speech recognition. The memo mode records the
audio, turns it into text and a summary, and inserts them as a voice-memo
block. Under the local-only AI policy this runs on your device; nothing is
sent anywhere. A pill at the bottom shows that the microphone is on; its
stop button ends the recording.

## Canvas

A whiteboard beside your notes: sticky notes, text, shapes, arrows,
frames and images on an infinite canvas, with pan, zoom, undo and redo.
Each canvas is saved in the vault as a `.tldr` file and saved again as you
draw.

## Sync conflicts

When the same note changed on this device and in the cloud since the
last sync, Lumen shows both versions side by side. Changes that don't
overlap are merged for you; for each part that does, choose this device's
or the cloud's version. You can also keep one side as a whole, or cancel
and decide later.

## Dialogs

Questions and confirmations open as small dialogs. **Enter** confirms,
**Escape** cancels, and focus goes back to where it was.

pages.md:
Lumen works by touch on phones and tablets, in Hebrew and in English.

## Dragging

Everything that drags with a mouse also drags with a finger or a pen:

- **Blocks in the rich editor.** Touch a block to show its handle, press the
  handle, slide, and lift where the block should go.
- **Tabs.** Press and hold a tab for a moment (about 0.4 s) to pick it up,
  slide it along the strip and lift to drop it. A quick swipe still scrolls
  the tab strip.
- **The sidebar edge.** Drag it to make the sidebar narrower or wider.
- **The graph view.** Tap a note's dot to open it; a finger has a wider hit
  area than the cursor.
- **Menus.** The slash menu, the formatting bubble and the AI button react to
  a tap the same way as to a click, and a tap outside closes them.

## Touch targets

On touch screens every button in the title bar, the status bar, toolbars and
the tab strip is at least **44 × 44** points, the size Apple and Google
recommend. The block handle grows to the same size.

## The notch and the home indicator

On phones with a notch or rounded corners Lumen uses the whole screen and
keeps the title bar and the status bar out of the notch, the corners and the
home indicator.

## The outline on a phone

On a narrow screen the outline is a **bottom sheet** instead of a side panel.
Open it from the command palette (*View → Outline*); picking a heading jumps
there and closes the sheet, and the ✕ button closes it too. Closing the
sheet on a phone does not change the side-panel setting on a wider screen.

## How it is tested

`e2e/touch.spec.ts` runs the full journey on an **iPhone 14** and a
**Pixel 7** profile (viewport, pixel ratio, touch input and the mobile user
agent): the safe-area viewport, the 44-pixel check on every control, typing,
the outline sheet, reordering tabs by long press, moving a block by its
handle. Opening a graph node by tap (a finger's wider hit area, no hover
before the tap) is a unit test in `src/__tests__/GraphViewRender.test.tsx`. Both profiles run on Chromium; Safari's
own engine is not part of the local run.

## Touch targets

On touch screens every button in the title bar, the status bar, toolbars and
the tab strip is at least **44 × 44** points, the size Apple and Google

## The notch and the home indicator

home indicator.

## The outline on a phone

On a narrow screen the outline is a **bottom sheet** instead of a side panel.
Open it from the command palette (*View → Outline*); picking a heading jumps
there and closes the sheet, and the ✕ button closes it too. Closing the
sheet on a phone does not change the side-panel setting on a wider screen.

## The editing toolbar

While you type on a phone or a tablet, a row of buttons sits on top of the
on-screen keyboard. It starts with the actions people reach for most:

- **⇥ / ⇤** indent and outdent the line (every selected line, lists
  included);
- **☐** turns the line into a task; tap again to check it, a third time to
  make it plain text again;
- **🔗** makes a link: selected text becomes its label, a selected address
  its target;
- **🖼** inserts a photo or an image from your files, stored in the vault
  like a pasted image;
- **H** makes a heading (tap again for a smaller one), **B** bold, **•** a
  bulleted list, **[[** a link to another note: type a few letters of its
  name and pick it from the list;
- **↶** undoes; **⌄** hides the keyboard.

Each button is one step: one undo takes it back. The row is 44 points high
like every touch target, scrolls sideways when it is longer than the
screen, and in Hebrew starts at the right, with its arrows pointing the way
the text moves.

### Making it yours

Tap **⋯** at the end of the row (or run *Customize the mobile toolbar* from
the command palette) to add actions (italic, numbered list, tag, code,
quote, redo and more), remove them, and move them with the ↑ and ↓ buttons.
**Reset** brings back the default row.

## Swipes

- Swipe in from the **start edge** of the screen for the file list, and from
  the **end edge** for the outline. "Start" follows the language: in Hebrew
  the file list comes in from the right, in English from the left.
- Swipe a panel back towards its edge to close it.

Only a swipe that starts within about 28 pixels of the edge counts, so
selecting text and scrolling a wide table work as before.

## Long notes open for reading

On a phone, a note of 600 words or more opens in reading view, so it's
quick to open and you don't bring up the keyboard by accident. **Tap the
text** to start editing: the editor opens with the cursor on the line you
tapped. Links, checkboxes, buttons and embeds still do what they do. Turn
this off with *Phone: open long notes for reading* in the command palette.

## Fewer taps

Ten common actions, in taps from an open note (a swipe or picking from a
list counts as one; typing a name doesn't):

| Action | Lumen | Obsidian Mobile | In Lumen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Turn a line into a task | 1 | 1 | toolbar ☐ |
| Indent a list item | 1 | 1 | toolbar ⇥ |
| Outdent a list item | 1 | 1 | toolbar ⇤ |
| Link to another note | 2 | 2 | toolbar [[, pick the note |
| Insert a photo | 2 | 2 | toolbar 🖼, pick the photo |
| Make the line a heading | 1 | 2 | toolbar H |
| Bold a word | 2 | 2 | double-tap the word, toolbar B |
| Open the file list | 1 | 1 | swipe in from the start edge |
| Open the outline | 1 | 2 | swipe in from the end edge |
| Start editing a long note at a paragraph | 1 | 2 | tap the paragraph |

The Obsidian Mobile column is counted by hand from its default toolbar and
gestures; it has not yet been measured on a device.

## How it is tested

`e2e/touch.spec.ts` runs the full journey on an **iPhone 14** and a
**Pixel 7** profile (viewport, pixel ratio, touch input and the mobile user
agent): the safe-area viewport, the 44-pixel check on every control, typing,
the outline sheet, reordering tabs by long press, moving a block by its
handle. Opening a graph node by tap (a finger's wider hit area, no hover
before the tap) is a unit test in `src/__tests__/GraphViewRender.test.tsx`. Both profiles run on Chromium; Safari's
own engine is not part of the local run.

`e2e/mobile-native.spec.ts` runs the phone editing journey on the same two
profiles, in Hebrew: the toolbar above the editor and its actions, the
customize sheet, both edge swipes mirrored, a long note opening for reading
and a tap landing on its line, and the time from launch to the last note.
The toolbar's text actions, the swipe rules and the tap-count table are
unit tests in `src/__tests__/mobileNative.test.ts`.

pages.md:
Lumen is one tap away on the phone, in Hebrew and in English.

## On the home screen

The **Lumen widget** (iPhone and Android) has three buttons:

- **Search** opens search.
- **Quick note** opens the quick-capture box with the cursor in it.
- **Today** opens today's daily note.

The widget shows no note text. In Hebrew the buttons run right to left.

## Siri, Spotlight and Shortcuts (iPhone)

These work without setup. Say them to Siri, type them in Spotlight, or
find them in the Shortcuts app:

| Say or search | What happens |
|---|---|
| "Add to Lumen inbox" | Siri asks what to add and adds it to the end of `inbox.md`, without opening Lumen |
| "Quick note in Lumen" | opens the quick-capture box |
| "Voice note in Lumen" | opens the box, recording |
| "Search Lumen" | opens search (and, from Shortcuts, with your query) |
| "Today's Lumen note" | opens today's note |

In Hebrew: "הוסף לתיבת הלכידה של Lumen", "פתק מהיר ב-Lumen", "חפש
ב-Lumen" and so on.

*Add to inbox* works even when Lumen is closed. The text waits on the
phone, and the next time Lumen opens it lands in `inbox.md` with the time
you said it. Each line is added once, and nothing is lost if Lumen is
closed again first.

## App Shortcuts (Android)

Long-press the Lumen icon: **Quick note**, **Voice note**, **Search** and
**Today**. Drag one to the home screen to keep it there.

## Links for other apps

Every widget button and shortcut is a link, which other apps and
automations can use too:

| Link | What it does |
|---|---|
| `lumen://capture` | opens the quick-capture box |
| `lumen://capture?mode=voice` | opens the box, recording |
| `lumen://capture?text=…` | adds the text to the inbox |
| `lumen://new` | opens a new note |

     `AppShortcuts.strings`).

   later).

The plan asks for these to be done and written down, on an iPhone and an
Android phone, with the phone in Hebrew and then in English:

   *Quick note* on the widget, and count frames from the tap to the
   blinking cursor. The app also logs `widget tap → typing` from the moment
   it receives the link, which leaves out the system's launch time.

   closed. Open Lumen: the sentence is at the end of `inbox.md`, with the
   time you said it.

   and the labels are in Hebrew. The same holds for the App Shortcuts.

   with "test".

pages.title: Beta channel and feature flags
pages.description: Try new features before everyone else, on the web or in the desktop app, and turn any beta feature on or off on your own device.
pages.md:
New features reach a **beta** first, then a stable release after testing.

## The beta

- **On the web:** the beta is a separate site, built from the same code,
  with new features turned on. A **Beta** badge in the status bar shows you
  are on it. Your notes stay in your browser as usual: the beta and the
  stable site are separate origins and don't share storage. To move notes
  between them, keep the vault in a folder on disk and open that folder in
  both, or export from one and import into the other.
- **In the desktop app:** command palette → **Update channel: switch between stable and beta**. Beta also
  installs beta releases; stable installs only tested releases. If you go
  back to stable, you stay on your current version until a stable release
  is newer, because the app never installs an older version.

Betas are numbered like `0.2.0-beta.1`. Once a beta has been tested, the
same changes ship as `0.2.0`.

## Feature flags

Each feature in beta has a flag. Command palette → **Feature flags…**
(or tap the **Beta** badge) lists them:

- **On or off:** turn any flag on or off for yourself. In a stable build
  you can try a beta feature; in a beta build you can turn one off.
- **Where the value comes from:** *Default for this build*, or *Your
  choice*, with a link back to the default. **Reset all** clears your
  choices.
- **Private:** flags are local. Lumen doesn't fetch them from a server and
  doesn't report them anywhere. Your choices stay in this browser or app.

Features in beta now:

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| Check for updates at launch | Desktop app: looks for a new version once a day when Lumen starts, so beta fixes arrive quickly. Never in *local only* mode; every check is in the privacy log. |

## How a feature graduates

A feature ships first in a beta with its flag on. A later release promotes
the flag to stable, and the feature is on for everyone. The project's
release check refuses a flag that reaches stable without an earlier beta.

pages.title: The desktop app
pages.description: Windows, tabs you drag between them, the tray with quick capture, opening .md files from Finder or Explorer, and lumen:// links.
pages.md:
The desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux) works like a native one.

## Windows and tabs

- **New window:** *File → New window* (⌘⇧N / Ctrl+Shift+N), or *New
  window* in the command palette. Every window shows the same vault and
  keeps its own tabs.
- **Move a tab:** drag it out of the tab strip and drop it on another
  window. Drop it outside every window to get a new window with that tab.
  The tab keeps its editing state: unsaved text, cursor and selection,
  scroll position and view mode. Undo history starts fresh in the new
  window.
- The move is safe: the first window keeps the tab until the second one
  has it open. If the second window closes first, nothing is lost.
- When you close an extra window, its tabs close with it. The main window
  remembers its tabs for the next launch.

## The tray

The Lumen icon in the menu bar (macOS) or the system tray (Windows, Linux)
has:

- **Quick capture…:** a small window. Type a thought and press Enter, and
  it is added to `inbox.md` with the date and time. Shift+Enter starts a
  new line, and Esc closes the window.
- **New note**, your **recent notes**, **Show Lumen** and **Quit Lumen**.

The menu follows the app's language.

## Opening files

Lumen registers itself for **`.md`** (and `.markdown`), **`.base`**
(database views) and **`.excalidraw`** (drawings). Double-click one in
Finder, Explorer or your file manager, or use *Open with → Lumen*, or run
`lumen note.md` in a terminal:

- **A file inside a vault** opens in that vault. If it belongs to a vault
  you used before, Lumen switches to it first. With vaults inside each
  other, the innermost one wins.
- **A file outside every vault** opens on its own. Saving writes it back
  to the same file, and nothing else on the disk becomes reachable.
- If Lumen is already running, the file opens in the running app. A second
  copy of Lumen is not started.

## Links: `lumen://`

| Link | What it does |
|---|---|
| `lumen://open?path=notes/idea.md` | opens a note of the current vault |
| `lumen://open?path=notes/idea.md&vault=Research` | opens it in the vault whose folder is named *Research* |
| `lumen://open?path=notes/idea.md&line=12` | opens it with the cursor on line 12 |
| `lumen://new` | opens a new note |
| `lumen://new?title=Idea&text=First%20line&folder=inbox` | opens a new note with that title and text; it isn't saved until you save it |
| `lumen://capture?text=Buy%20milk` | adds a line to `inbox.md` |

Encode values as you would in a URL. Hebrew works: `lumen://open?path=%D7%A8%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%95%D7%9F.md`.

Links are checked strictly, because a link can come from anywhere:

- `path` is inside the vault: no `..`, no absolute path, no drive letter;
- `vault` matches only a vault you opened before; a link can never point
  Lumen at a new folder;
- `new` opens an unsaved note, so nothing is written that you haven't seen.

To make a link from a page or a script, use the path relative to the vault
folder, with forward slashes.

## How it is tested

The shell's decisions are covered by tests in `src-tauri/desktop`
(`cargo test --offline --manifest-path src-tauri/desktop/Cargo.toml`). It
is plain Rust with no dependencies, and the tests cover:

- link parsing, including every way to escape the vault;
- which vault holds a file, with nested vaults, `..`, and case on macOS and
  Windows;
- launch arguments;
- where a dropped tab lands, and the two-phase move (never lost, never
  doubled);
- the tray menu and quick-capture entries.

The WebView side is covered by `src/__tests__/desktopShell.test.ts`.

What needs a person, on each of macOS, Windows and Linux:

1. Double-click a `.md` file in a vault you used before: Lumen opens in
   that vault, on that note.
2. Double-click a `.md` file outside every vault: it opens on its own, and
   saving changes the file.
3. Open `lumen://open?path=…` from a browser: the note opens. Then open
   `lumen://capture?text=test`: `inbox.md` gains a line.
4. Drag a tab with unsaved text to a second window: the text, cursor and
   scroll come along, and the first window no longer has the tab.
5. Tray → *Quick capture…* in Hebrew: the window is right to left, and
   Enter adds the line to the inbox.

pages.title: Desktop app updates
pages.description: How the Lumen desktop app checks for, verifies and installs updates, and what it sends.
pages.md:
The desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) updates itself from the project's
GitHub releases.

- **Check:** command palette → **Check for updates…**. A stable build never
  checks on its own. A beta build checks once a day at launch, unless you
  turn that off under [feature flags](/getting-started/beta/).
- **Channel:** command palette → **Update channel: switch between stable and beta** switches between stable
  and beta releases ([beta channel](/getting-started/beta/)).
- **What is sent:** one request to the release server with the app version
  and platform. No notes, no account, no identifier. It appears in the
  privacy log.
- **Local only:** when the privacy policy is *local only*, nothing is
  checked. The command says so instead.
- **Verification:** every update is signed. The app checks the signature
  against the key built into it and refuses a file that doesn't match, or an
  older version presented as new.
- **Install:** after you confirm, Lumen downloads, verifies, installs and restarts.

A build without the update key (local and development builds) has no
updater. *Check for updates…* says it isn't configured, and new versions are
installed by hand.

## Signed installers

Release installers are code-signed once the project's signing certificates
are in place (Windows Authenticode, Apple Developer ID). Until then Windows
SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper show a warning on first launch.

## What the app is allowed to do

The window has no general file-system permission. It reaches only the vault
folder you picked, through Lumen's own commands. No shell, no arbitrary
HTTP from the native side, and no source maps in the shipped files.

pages.title: Send feedback
pages.description: Report a bug, an idea or a question as a GitHub issue or as text to copy. Lumen has no feedback server, and nothing is sent until you click.
pages.md:
Open it with `⌘K → Help: Send feedback`, or with **Report a problem…** at the
bottom of the [AI doctor](/ai/doctor/).

Lumen has no feedback server. The form turns what you write into the text of
a GitHub issue, and you choose what happens to it:

- **Open on GitHub** opens github.com in a new tab with the issue form filled
  in (title, text and a label for the kind). You check it there and submit it.
  You need a GitHub account.
- **Copy text** puts the same text on your clipboard, for an e-mail or
  anywhere else.

Until you click one of those two buttons, nothing leaves your device. The form
makes no network request, and the preview shows exactly the text that will be
sent.

## What goes in

| Part | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| Kind, title, description | always | what you wrote |
| App and browser details | ticked (the default) | Lumen version; web, installed app or desktop; platform; language; AI policy; the browser's user agent |
| AI doctor report | only when you tick it | the doctor's checks of the local AI stack. It never contains note text. Keys, tokens, passwords in URLs and e-mail addresses are removed before it goes in. |
| Screenshot | only when you take one | never part of the text (see below) |

If the issue text is too long for a link, GitHub opens with the title only and
the text is on your clipboard: paste it into the issue.

## Screenshots

**Save a screenshot to attach** asks your browser to capture a screen, window or
tab. The browser shows its own prompt, so you choose what is captured. The
picture is saved on your computer as `lumen-feedback-<date>-<time>.png`. It is
not uploaded. Attach it to the GitHub issue yourself. It may show your notes,
so look at it first.

Browsers without screen capture (most phones) say so and skip this step.

## Diagnostics file

**Save diagnostics** (in the feedback form, on an error screen, or **Save a
diagnostics file** in the command palette) saves `lumen-diagnostics-<date>.json`
on your computer, for you to attach to the issue. It holds what a maintainer
needs to understand a problem, and nothing about what you wrote:

- the version, the app shell (web, installed, desktop), the platform and
  the browser;
- your settings, copied one by one from a fixed list: switches, modes and
  sizes. No note names, folders, keys, tokens or e-mail addresses;
- the vault counted, not read: how many notes, other files and folders, and
  their total size;
- storage: whether the vault is in the browser's private storage, and how
  full it is;
- the last warnings and errors, with every path, URL path, quoted text,
  address and key in them replaced by a placeholder.

Before the file is saved, Lumen checks it once more against the text it
holds in memory (your notes, their names, your keys), and refuses to save a
file that would contain any of it.

## Help in the app

**Help** in the command palette (or F1) opens this documentation inside
Lumen. It is packed into the app, so it works offline, and its search
handles Hebrew prefixes as the website's search does. Every panel and
dialog has a **?** button that opens the help at the part about it.

sections.text: Save a screenshot to attach asks your browser to capture a screen, window or tab. The browser shows its own prompt, so you choose what is captured. The picture is saved on your computer as lumen-feedback- - .png. It is not uploaded. Attach it to the GitHub issue yourself. It may show your notes, so look at it first. Browsers without screen capture (most phones) say so and skip this step.

sections.heading: Diagnostics file
sections.text: Save diagnostics (in the feedback form, on an error screen, or Save a diagnostics file in the command palette) saves lumen-diagnostics- .json on your computer, for you to attach to the issue. It holds what a maintainer needs to understand a problem, and nothing about what you wrote: the version, the app shell (web, installed, desktop), the platform and the browser; your settings, copied one by one from a fixed list: switches, modes and sizes. sections.text: Help in the command palette (or F1) opens this documentation inside Lumen. It is packed into the app, so it works offline, and its search handles Hebrew prefixes as the website's search does. Every panel and dialog has a ? button that opens the help at the part about it.

pages.md:
## Export from Notion

1. In Notion: **Settings → Export** (a single page: **⋯ → Export**).
2. Choose **Markdown & CSV**, include subpages, and download the .zip.

## Bring it in

`⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`, then pick the

- removes the IDs from file and folder names (`Plans 1a2b….md` → `Plans.md`);

| Toggles, callouts | Markdown lists and blockquotes |
| Comments, page history, permissions | not in the export |

pages.title: Moving from Obsidian
pages.description: Bring an Obsidian vault into Lumen — notes, attachments, links and Bases — and what changes on the way.
pages.md:
An Obsidian vault is a folder of Markdown files, and so is a Lumen vault:
nothing has to be converted.

## Bring the vault in

1. In Obsidian nothing needs exporting. Zip the vault folder, or keep it as
   a folder.
2. In Lumen: `⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`
   and pick the .zip or the folder.
3. Lumen recognises the vault by its `.obsidian/` folder and imports every
   note and attachment into a new folder, `Imported/<vault name>`. Nothing
   that is already in Lumen is overwritten. Obsidian's own settings
   (`.obsidian/`, `.trash/`) stay behind.

Details and the full list of what is skipped: [Export and
import](/workspace/export-import/).

## What carries over

| In Obsidian | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| `[[wikilinks]]`, `[[note#heading]]`, `![[embeds]]` | the same syntax |
| Frontmatter properties, `tags:` | the same YAML; the tags panel and database views read it |
| Attachments (images, PDFs) | the same files, the same relative links |
| Callouts `> [!note]` | shown as a quote; Lumen's callouts are `:::note` blocks |
| Canvas (`.canvas`) | kept as files |
| Plugins and themes | not carried over: Lumen has its own [plugins](/plugins/sdk/) |

## Daily habits

- **Command palette**: `⌘K`, as `⌘P` in Obsidian. [Keyboard
  shortcuts](/getting-started/shortcuts/) lists the rest.
- **Hebrew**: the editor and preview are right-to-left aware per paragraph;
  see [Hebrew and right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/).
- **Sync**: Obsidian Sync does not reach Lumen. Use Git, or keep the vault
  in a folder both apps open on the desktop.

## Going back

Your notes stay plain Markdown. `⌘K → Export the whole vault…` gives you a
.zip or a folder that Obsidian opens as a vault.

pages.title: Install with a package manager
pages.description: Install the Lumen desktop app with Homebrew, winget, Flatpak or the AUR, and where those packages come from.
pages.md:
Each release of the desktop app is published as a GitHub release. The
Homebrew cask, the winget manifests, the Flathub manifest and the AUR
package are all generated from that release's `SHA256SUMS`, so every
channel installs the same files.

| System | Command |
|---|---|
| macOS (Homebrew) | `brew install --cask lumen-md` |
| Windows (winget) | `winget install Talstilkol.Lumen` |
| Linux (Flathub) | `flatpak install flathub io.github.talstilkol.Lumen` |
| Arch Linux (AUR) | `yay -S lumen-md-bin` (or any AUR helper) |

A channel works once the owner has submitted that release to it. Until
then, download the installer from the GitHub release and check it with
`SHA256SUMS`.

## Updates

- Homebrew, winget, Flatpak and the AUR update the app like any other
  package.
- The app's own updater ([Desktop app updates](/getting-started/desktop-updates/))
  stays on, and checks the same signed release.

## The Flatpak sandbox

The Flatpak app may use the network (sync, model downloads, and cloud AI
when you allow it) and your `Documents` folder. A vault in any other
folder opens through the system's file picker, which grants access to
that folder only.

## For maintainers

`node scripts/release.mjs packages` writes every manifest and checks it
offline. See `RELEASE.md`, "Stores and package managers".

pages.title: Install Lumen
pages.description: Lumen in the browser, as an installed web app, on the desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) and on iOS / Android — and what each one stores where.
pages.md:
Lumen is the same app on every platform. The only differences are where
your notes are kept and how the app is updated.

| Platform | How | Notes are kept in |
|---|---|---|
| Browser | open the hosted app, or `npm run dev` from a clone | the browser's private file system (OPFS) |
| Installed web app (PWA) | the browser's **Install** button on the hosted app | the same OPFS; works offline |
| macOS / Windows / Linux | build with `npm run tauri:build` (Tauri 2) | a real folder on disk |
| iOS | `npm run ios:open` (Capacitor, opens Xcode) | the app's storage |
| Android | `npm run android:open` (Capacitor, opens Android Studio) | the app's storage |

## In the browser

Nothing to install. Notes stay in this browser's private storage and never
leave the device unless you turn on sync. **Clearing the site's data
deletes them**, so export the vault (*Export the whole vault…*, see
[Export and import](/workspace/export-import/)) before you clear
browser data, or keep the vault in a real folder.

The minimum versions (set by Tailwind CSS 4) are Safari and iOS 16.4+,
Chrome / Edge 111+ and Firefox 128+.

## Installed web app (offline)

Use the browser's install button (Chrome, Edge) or *Share → Add to Home
Screen* (Safari). The installed app opens without a network: the editor,
highlighting, fonts and your files are all cached.

## Desktop

There are no signed release builds yet, so build from a clone:

```bash
npm ci
npm run tauri:build
```

The desktop app keeps the vault as a folder of plain `.md` files that
other tools (git, Obsidian, a text editor) can open, and keeps secrets in
the OS keychain on macOS and Windows (see
[How Lumen stores your secrets](/security/vault/)). On Linux it needs
WebKitGTK 2.40+.

## iOS and Android

The mobile projects are generated with Capacitor:

```bash
npm ci
npm run ios:open        # or: npm run android:open
```

Then build and run from Xcode or Android Studio.

## Running from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run dev
```

pages.title: Quickstart
pages.description: Get to your first beautiful Lumen document in 60 seconds.
pages.md:
## 1. Open Lumen

Either visit [lumen.app](https://lumen.app) (the hosted PWA), install the
desktop app (see [Install Lumen](/getting-started/install/)), or run
locally:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## 2. Type your first note

Hit `⌘N` for a fresh document. Try the smart paste — `⌘⇧V` opens an
"Insert anything…" dialog. Drop in:

- a YouTube link → it wraps as `\`\`\`embed`
- a CSV row → it wraps as `\`\`\`csv` and shows a sortable table + chart
  suggestions
- a SQL `CREATE TABLE` → ditto, parsed as data
- Mermaid `flowchart LR …` → renders as SVG
- A LaTeX equation → math typeset by KaTeX

## 3. Save it

`⌘S` saves to your local OPFS workspace. Open the workspace pane
(`⌘K → Toggle workspace`) to browse / rename / move files. Everything is
just markdown — your notes remain portable.

## 4. Power-user keys

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `⌘K` | Command palette (everything is here) |
| `⇧⌘F` | Focus mode |
| `⌘⇧V` | Smart Insert (auto-detect) |
| `⌘1`–`⌘4` | Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG |
| `⌘H` | Find and replace |
| `⌘O` / `⌘N` | Open / New |

Workspace search is `⌘K → Search workspace…`; the full list is on
[Keyboard shortcuts](/getting-started/shortcuts/).

Now start writing — and explore the [Editor modes](/editor/modes/) for the
heavier surfaces.

pages.title: Welcome to Lumen
pages.description: Why we built Lumen, and what makes it different from Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear.
pages.md:
## Where Lumen fits

There's no shortage of markdown editors — Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear,
Logseq, Roam, HackMD, Joplin, Craft. Lumen sits at a specific intersection:

| | Lumen | Obsidian | Notion | Typora | Bear |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Local-first (works offline) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Web app (no install) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Auto data → table + chart | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ DB only | ❌ | ❌ |
| RTL / Hebrew first-class | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ |
| Mermaid + Graphviz + PlantUML + ABC + 3D | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ Mermaid only | ⚠️ | ❌ |
| Real-time collab | ✅ WebRTC | ❌ | ✅ Pro | ❌ | ❌ |
| Smart search (embeddings) | ✅ Pro | ⚠️ plugin | ✅ AI | ❌ | ❌ |
| MCP for AI agents | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Local LLM (WebGPU) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Open source (MIT) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

## What we believe

**1. Plain text wins.** Lumen never invents a proprietary format — every
note is portable markdown. Rendering is opinionated; storage isn't.

**2. Data is content.** A spreadsheet inside a note shouldn't need a
plugin. Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and it just becomes a table with
chart suggestions.

**3. AI assists, never gates.** Bring your own key. Disable AI entirely
and Lumen still ships every other feature.

**4. Privacy is structural, not promised.** Local-first storage, transport-encrypted
(WebRTC DTLS) collab, opt-in telemetry that's off by default.

Continue to the [Quickstart](/getting-started/quickstart/) →

pages.title: What's new
pages.description: After an update, Lumen shows that version's release notes once, in your interface language.
pages.md:
When Lumen updates, the next time you open it you see **What's new**: that
version's release notes, in the language of your interface. They appear
**once per version**. A new install doesn't show them, since nothing is new
to you yet.

To read them again at any time, run `⌘K → "What's new in this version"`.

The notes ship inside the app, so they work offline.

## For maintainers: where the notes come from

- **English** is `CHANGELOG.md`, which `node scripts/release.mjs prepare`
  writes from the commit subjects (see `RELEASE.md`). Commit links and
  scopes are left out of what readers see.
- **Other languages** live in `changelog/<locale>.md`, for example
  `changelog/he.md`, with the same `## [x.y.z] - date` sections.
  `release.mjs prepare` copies each new English section into every file
  there, marked `<!-- untranslated -->`.
- To translate a release, translate the section and delete that line.
  Until then the app shows the English notes under the language's own
  headings, and says they aren't translated yet.

pages.md:
## What makes Lumen different


  
    Your notes live in your browser's OPFS. Sync with Git, Dropbox, or your own
    server. Or don't sync at all — Lumen works fully offline.
  
  
    Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and Lumen suggests the right chart with one
    click. Live data via `src=` URLs that auto-refresh.
  
  
    Mermaid · Graphviz · PlantUML · KaTeX · ABC notation · model-viewer ·
    Leaflet maps · ECharts. All first-class.
  
  
    Hebrew and Arabic flow right-to-left throughout the UI. Code blocks, math,
    and the editor stay LTR.
  
  
    Smart search, auto-tagging, link suggestions. Bring your OpenAI key, or
    flip to local LLM (web-llm + WebGPU) — your prompts never leave your
    machine.
  
  
    Lumen ships an MCP server so Claude Desktop / Cursor can read, write, and
    search your workspace through `npx @lumen-md/mcp-server`.
  


## Three lines to get going

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md && npm ci && npm run dev
# open http://localhost:5173
```

Or just visit [lumen.app](https://lumen.app) and start typing — there's
nothing to install.

pages.title: Plugin API
pages.description: The lumen object a sandboxed plugin gets — every method, the capability it needs, its limits, and the UI elements.
pages.md:
A plugin's `main` is an ES module that runs in the sandbox (see
[Sandbox and permissions](/plugins/sandbox/)). It talks to Lumen only
through the global `lumen` object. Every method returns a promise. A
method whose capability you were not granted rejects with a `PluginDenied`
error.

## Events

```js
const off = lumen.on(name, (payload) => { … }); // off() unsubscribes
```

| Event | When | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `command:<id>` | One of your commands ran | `{ source: "palette" }` |
| `render:<lang>` | A ```` ```<lang> ```` block needs rendering | `{ requestId, source }` |
| `ui:panel` / `ui:block` | A button was clicked or a field changed in your panel / block | `{ id, kind: "click" \| "change", value? }` |
| `panel:closed` | The user closed your panel | — |

Your handlers get 250 ms of CPU each time they are called. Waiting for a
`lumen.*` call does not count toward that.

## Methods

| Method | Capability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `document.getText()` / `getFileName()` / `getSelection()` | `document:read` | `getSelection()` → `{ from, to, text }` or `null` |
| `document.setText(text)` / `insertText(text)` / `replaceSelection(text)` | `document:write` | Insert replaces the selection at the cursor |
| `vault.list(dir?)` / `vault.read(path)` | `vault:read` | Relative paths only: no `..` and no hidden folders. Reads are capped at 5 MB |
| `vault.write(path, text)` | `vault:write` | `.md`, `.txt`, `.json` or `.csv` only, 5 MB at most |
| `commands.register({ id, label, hint? }, handler?)` / `commands.unregister(id)` | `commands` | Up to 50 per plugin. The label shows "· your plugin name" |
| `panel.open({ title? })` / `panel.render(tree)` / `panel.close()` | `panel` | One plugin panel at a time |
| `renderer.register(lang)` / `renderer.result(requestId, tree)` | `renderer` | Up to 10 languages. Languages Lumen renders itself (`mermaid`, `chart`, `csv`, …) are refused |
| `settings.get()` / `settings.set(object)` | `settings` | Your own JSON, 64 KB at most |
| `storage.get(key)` / `set(key, value)` / `delete(key)` | `storage` | Your own key–value store: 1,000 keys of at most 1 MB each. Removed when you are uninstalled |
| `clipboard.writeText(text)` | `clipboard:write` | — |
| `notifications.show(text, "info" \| "success" \| "error")` | `notifications` | Shown with your name in front |
| `network.fetch(url, { method?, headers?, body? })` | `network:<origin>` | Only to the exact origin you were granted. No cookies, no redirects, 30 s timeout, 5 MB at most. Returns `{ status, headers, body }`. Recorded in the privacy ledger; blocked under local-only |
| `bases.query(path, view?, { offset?, limit? })` | `bases:read` | A `.base` view's rows, as the app shows them: `{ view, columns, rows: [{ path, cells }], total, errors }`. Cells are JSON (dates as ISO text, links as paths). At most 10,000 rows per call |
| `bases.update([{ path, set: { property: value } }])` | `bases:write` | Changes note properties. **One approval screen covers the whole call**: the user sees how many notes, which properties and the first five, and nothing is written unless they allow it. At most 5,000 rows. Returns `{ written, unchanged, declined }` |
| `lumen.manifest` | — | Your manifest (read-only) |

`console.log` / `warn` / `error` are allowed, up to 120 lines a minute.

## UI elements

Panels and rendered blocks are **trees of these elements**, and nothing
else:

`text {text}` · `heading {level 1–3, text}` · `paragraph {children}` ·
`box {direction "row"|"column", gap, children}` · `list {ordered, items: [[…]]}` ·
`button {id, label, primary?, disabled?}` · `input {id, value?, placeholder?, multiline?}` ·
`checkbox {id, label, checked?}` · `select {id, value?, options: [{value, label}]}` ·
`code {text, lang?}` · `noteLink {target, label?}` (a note in the vault, never a URL) · `divider`

A tree can have at most 2,000 nodes, nest at most 24 levels deep, and hold
at most 20,000 characters of text per node. An unknown element or field is
refused.

## Examples

The examples live in `public/plugins/examples/`:

- `word-stats` — a command, a panel, settings, `document:read`
- `callout` — a code-block renderer that keeps checklist ticks in `storage`

pages.title: Developing a plugin
pages.description: Scaffold a sandboxed plugin with create-lumen-plugin, run it with hot reload in developer mode, test it in Node with the test kit, and see what it does in the Developer panel.
pages.md:
## Five minutes from nothing to a running plugin

```bash
npx create-lumen-plugin my-plugin
cd my-plugin
npm run dev        # http://127.0.0.1:5199, watches the folder
```

1. In Lumen open **Plugin gallery**, then **Developer mode** at the bottom.
   Keep `http://127.0.0.1:5199` and press **Connect**.
2. Run the command your plugin registers from `⌘K` (in the template: *My plugin*): the side panel shows the word count of the note.
3. Change `main.js` and save. Lumen reloads the plugin by itself, usually
   in well under a second. The panel shows how long the last reload took.

Nothing needs installing: the dev server and the test kit use only Node
(20 or later).

## What is in the folder

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `lumen-plugin.json` | The manifest: id, name, version, and the capabilities the plugin asks for, each with the reason the user sees. |
| `main.js` | The plugin. It runs in the [sandbox](/plugins/sandbox/): only the `lumen` API, no DOM, no network unless asked for. |
| `test/main.test.mjs` | Tests, run with `npm test`. |
| `tools/dev-server.mjs` | The dev server behind `npm run dev`. |
| `tools/testkit.mjs` | The test kit. |

## Developer mode

Developer mode loads the plugin from the dev server instead of the
gallery:

- It connects only to this computer (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`).
- Keep the dev server on port 5199: the app's content security policy
  allows that port on this computer and no other.
- The plugin gets the capabilities its manifest asks for, without the
  permission screen: it is your own code.
- Each version is still run through the [safety scan](/plugins/permissions/),
  and the panel shows its notes. The scan's verdict does not block your own
  plugin here, but the gallery will not list a version that fails.
- On every save the dev server sends a `change` event and Lumen loads the
  manifest and `main.js` again. Changes that arrive during a reload are
  collected into one more reload.

## The Developer panel

While the plugin runs, the panel shows:

- **Reloads**: how many, how long the last one took (from the save to the
  plugin running again), and how long the start took.
- **CPU and memory**: the time spent in the plugin's code, how many runs,
  the longest, and the sandbox's memory.
- **Permissions: asked for and used**: each capability in the manifest,
  how often it was used and refused. A capability that is never used is
  marked: ask only for what you use, because users see the list before
  they install.
- **Last calls**: the plugin's last calls to Lumen, with their time and
  whether they were refused.

## Testing in Node

```js




test("shows the count", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", document: { text: "שלום עולם" } });
  await p.run("show");                       // a command it registered
  assert.equal(p.panel.tree.type, "box");    // the panel it rendered
});

test("needs document:read", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", grants: ["commands", "panel"] });
  await assert.rejects(p.run("show"), { name: "PluginDenied" });
});
```

`loadPlugin` runs `main.js` in a fresh Node `vm` context with a mock of the
`lumen` API. It follows the sandbox's rules: the same method table (a test
in Lumen keeps the two equal), a call without its capability rejects with
`PluginDenied`, and arguments must be JSON. The mock state is `document`
(`text`, `fileName`, `selection`), `vault` (`{"folder/note.md": text}`),
`settings`, `storage` and `fetch` for granted network calls.

You get back what the plugin did: `commands`, `panel`, `rendered`,
`document`, `vault`, `storage`, `notifications`, `clipboard`, `logs`,
`calls` and `denied`. You drive it with `run(id, payload)`,
`emit(name, payload)` (for example `"ui:panel"`), `render(lang, source)`
for a code-block renderer, and `select(from, to)`.

Node is not QuickJS, so test in Lumen too before you publish. Two
differences to keep in mind: QuickJS has no `Intl`, and the sandbox
limits CPU time and memory.

## Examples

The gallery's eight examples are in `public/plugins/examples/`:

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| Word stats | A panel, settings, Hebrew and English counting |
| Callout cards | A code-block renderer, storage |
| Quote of the day | Network access to one origin |
| Table of contents | Reading and writing the note |
| Hebrew date | A renderer and a command, a calendar computed without `Intl` |
| Tasks overview | Reading the whole vault (`vault:read`), a panel with note links |
| Bidi cleaner | Selection or whole note, notifications |
| Text format | A port of an Obsidian plugin (MIT), several commands |

## Publishing

Bump `version` in `lumen-plugin.json` and open a pull request that adds
the folder under `public/plugins/examples/` and a line in its
`index.json`. Run `node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` first: every version is
scanned, and a version that fails is not listed.

pages.title: Permissions and safety scan
pages.description: Before a sandboxed plugin installs, Lumen shows every permission it asks for in plain language; every version in the registry is scanned, and a version that fails is not shown.
pages.md:
A sandboxed plugin can do nothing until you allow it — see the
[plugin API](/plugins/api/). Two things make that choice informed.

## The install screen

**Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…** opens a screen that lists,
before anything runs, every permission the plugin's manifest asks for:

| Permission | What it lets the plugin do |
|---|---|
| `document:read` | Read the note that is open |
| `document:write` | Change the note that is open (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:read` | Read any note in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:write` | Create and change notes in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `commands` | Add commands to the command palette |
| `panel` | Show a side panel |
| `renderer` | Draw code blocks of its own language in the preview |
| `settings` | Keep its own settings |
| `storage` | Store its own data on this device |
| `clipboard:write` | Copy text to your clipboard (*sensitive*) |
| `notifications` | Show notifications |
| `network:<origin>` | Connect to that one address — and nowhere else (*sensitive*) |

Each line also shows the plugin's own reason (“Why: …”) and the version's
safety scan. **Install and allow** grants exactly what is listed; anything
else the plugin tries is refused by the sandbox, and every network request
appears in the privacy ledger. The code is scanned again right before it
runs, so the card can't describe a different copy.

## The safety scan

Every version in the registry (`public/plugins/examples/index.json`) is
scanned by `scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` into `scan.json`; the gallery shows
each version's card — a grade (A, B, C), a score out of 100, and what the
scan noted. **A version that fails is not shown and cannot be installed.**

The scan reads the code — it never runs it — and fails a version that:

- uses an API whose permission the manifest does not declare (for example
  writes to the note with only `document:read`);
- reaches the network without declaring it, or connects to an origin other
  than the one declared;
- runs code made from text (`eval`, `Function`, string timers), loads more
  code (`import`), or indexes `globalThis` / `lumen` with a computed key;
- is not valid JavaScript, is larger than 512 KB, or has a signature that
  does not verify.

It notes (and lowers the score for) permissions asked for but not used,
indirect use of the API, network addresses built while running, and a
missing or unknown signature.

To check a new version before publishing: add it to `index.json`, then
`node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` (or `--check` to only verify).

## Reporting a problem

Every card and install screen has **Report a problem**, which opens an issue
with the plugin's id and version filled in.

pages.md:
The **Sandboxed plugins** section of the Plugin Gallery lists plugins from a
static registry that ships with Lumen. There is no plugin server: the registry
is a folder of files, and every version in it passes the safety scan before it
is listed.

## The ten plugins

These are modelled on the kinds of Obsidian plugins people download most
(templates, task boards, calendars, tables, linting, tags, spaced repetition,
refactoring, dates, sorting). Each is written for Lumen's sandbox: none of them
uses the network, so they all work under the **local-only** AI policy.

| Plugin | What it does | Permissions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Templates** | Inserts a note from your `Templates` folder, filling `{{date}}`, `{{date:DD/MM/YYYY}}`, `{{time}}`, `{{title}}`, `{{selection}}`, `{{weekday}}` and `{{hebrewWeekday}}`. | commands, read the vault, read and change the open note, panel, settings |
| **Kanban board** | Draws a ` ```kanban ` block (a `## heading` per column, a `- item` per card) as columns, and copies the board as a Markdown table. | code-block renderer, commands, read and change the open note, clipboard, notifications |
| **Calendar** | A month view of your daily notes (`YYYY-MM-DD.md`). Days that have a note link to it. The week starts on Sunday, or on Monday if you choose. | commands, panel, read the vault, settings |
| **Table formatter** | Lines up the columns of every table and sorts a table by the column under the cursor. Hebrew niqqud takes no width. | commands, read and change the open note |
| **Markdown tidy** | Fixes trailing spaces, extra blank lines, heading spacing, mixed bullets and a missing final newline. It never touches code or front matter. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Tag manager** | Lists every `#tag` in the vault, Hebrew tags included, and renames a tag and its nested tags everywhere at once. | commands, panel, read and change the vault, notifications |
| **Flashcards** | Turns `question :: answer` lines into cards and schedules reviews with SM-2. The note itself is never changed. | commands, read the open note, panel, storage |
| **Note refactor** | Moves the selection into a new note and leaves a `[[link]]` in its place, or splits a note into one note per heading. | commands, read and change the open note, read and change the vault, notifications, settings |
| **Natural dates** | Turns “tomorrow”, “next Friday”, “in 3 days”, “מחר”, “יום שישי הבא” or 12/11/2026 (day first) into `[[2026-11-13]]`. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Sort lines** | Sorts the selected lines A→Z, Z→A or by length, reverses them, or removes duplicates. Sub-items stay with their item. Hebrew sorts by letter (final letters sort with their regular forms), and numbers sort by value. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications |

Install one from **Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…**. The
permission screen lists everything the plugin asks for and why. Once a plugin is
installed, its card shows **Remove**, which stops the plugin and deletes the
settings and data it stored.

The plugins write their labels in English and Hebrew, because the plugin API
does not tell a plugin which language the app is in.

## How the registry is built

```
public/plugins/examples/
  index.json          ← built: every plugin, its versions, the SHA-256 of each version's code
  scan.json           ← built: the safety scan of every version
  kanban/             ← one folder per version
    lumen-plugin.json
    main.js
```

```sh
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs           # rebuild index.json and scan.json
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --check   # fail if either is out of date or a version fails
```

The build does the following:

- validates every manifest;
- refuses stray files in a plugin folder (only the manifest, its entries, a `LICENSE` and a `README` are allowed);
- refuses an id and version that appear twice;
- writes `index.json`;
- scans every version (`scripts/scan-plugins.mjs`).

A new version goes in a folder of its own, for example `kanban@1.1.0`.

When you install a plugin, the app scans the downloaded code again. It refuses
the code if its SHA-256 differs from the hash in the registry scan.

## Not yet

- The plugins are **unsigned**, so their cards show the “unsigned” note.
  Signing them needs the owner's key; see [Plugin signing keys](/plugins/signing/).

pages.title: Plugin sandbox and permissions
pages.description: How Lumen runs plugins with no access by default — QuickJS for logic, UI as data, a capability list the user grants.
pages.md:
Lumen runs every plugin with **no access by default**. A plugin gets only
the capabilities you grant it when you install it, and you can revoke them
at any time.

## Where plugin code runs

| Part | Runs in | What it can reach |
|---|---|---|
| Logic (`main`) | [QuickJS](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten) (MIT), a separate JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly, inside its own Web Worker | Only the `lumen` object. There is no `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `importScripts`, DOM or storage, and no `import` of other modules. |
| Interface (panels, settings, block output) | Lumen itself | The plugin sends a **tree of known elements**: text, heading, paragraph, box, list, button, input, checkbox, select, code, link to a note, divider. There is no `img`, `iframe`, `form`, `style`, `script` or HTML, and no link to a web address. |

The interface is data rather than a sandboxed iframe on purpose. CSP and the
iframe `sandbox` attribute block every channel but one: a frame may always
navigate *itself* (`location = "https://…?" + text`). A tree of known
elements has no such channel.

## Limits

Each plugin has a 32 MB heap and a 512 KB stack. It gets 250 ms of CPU each
time Lumen enters its code (an event, the reply to a call), and its console
is capped at 120 lines a minute. A plugin that goes over a limit, or throws
an error nobody catches, is stopped.

## Capabilities

| Capability | Gives |
|---|---|
| `document:read` / `document:write` | The open note's text and selection / changing it |
| `vault:read` / `vault:write` | Listing and reading notes / writing notes |
| `commands` | Commands in the palette |
| `panel` | A side panel |
| `renderer` | Rendering a code-block language |
| `settings` | A settings section |
| `storage` | Its own key–value storage |
| `clipboard:write` | Copying text |
| `notifications` | Toasts |
| `network:https://exact.origin` | Requests to **that origin only** — https (http only for localhost), no cookies, no redirects, at most 5 MB of response |

Every capability the manifest asks for comes with a reason, which is shown
to you before you grant it. A call without its capability fails inside the
plugin with `PluginDenied` and never reaches Lumen. Lumen checks the grant
a second time on the host side, because the worker is a boundary, not the
policy.

## Network and privacy

Every request a plugin makes appears in the **privacy ledger** under
"Plugin". Under the **local-only** AI policy, plugin requests are blocked
and logged as blocked, even when the plugin has a network grant.

## Manifest (`lumen-plugin.json`)

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "org.example.word-stats",
  "name": "Word stats",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Counts words in the open note",
  "author": "Example",
  "license": "MIT",
  "main": "main.js",
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "document:read", "reason": "To count the words of the open note" },
    { "id": "commands", "reason": "Adds the “Word stats” command" }
  ]
}
```

pages.title: Plugin signing keys
pages.description: Decide which publishers' plugins Lumen trusts.
pages.md:
Registry plugins can be signed with an **Ed25519** key. Before installing,
Lumen verifies the signature against the keys you trust, so a compromised
CDN cannot ship modified code.

## Manage trusted keys

Command palette → **Trusted plugin signing keys…**

- **Built-in** keys come from the deployment (`VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS`)
  and cannot be removed from the UI.
- **Your keys** are stored in this browser. Paste the publisher's public key
  and press **Trust key**.

Each key is identified by its **fingerprint** — the SHA-256 of the public
key, in hex. Compare it with the fingerprint the publisher lists on their
website before trusting it.

## Accepted formats

- Base64 SPKI (44 bytes for Ed25519, starts with `MCow`).
- PEM: `-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- … -----END PUBLIC KEY-----`.

Generate a key pair with OpenSSL:

```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out plugin-signing.pem
openssl pkey -in plugin-signing.pem -pubout
```

## Errors

- **Not an Ed25519 public key** — the pasted text is not a 44-byte SPKI
  Ed25519 key (RSA and ECDSA keys are not accepted).
- **Untrusted signer** — the plugin is correctly signed, but by a key you
  have not trusted. Verify the fingerprint, then add the key.
